stage1_evidence_shown.label: OBJECTIVE
stage1_evidence_shown.context: To compare two treatment strategies in preterm infants with or at risk of respiratory distress syndrome: early surfactant administration (within one hour of birth) versus late surfactant administration, in a geographically defined population.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: OUTCOME
stage1_evidence_shown.context: The primary outcome was chronic lung disease (CLD) and mortality before/at 36 weeks. Secondary outcomes included: duration of mechanical ventilation and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), post-natal steroids for CLD and major neonatal morbidities.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: SUBJECTS
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Premature infants born at 22-32 weeks' gestation between January 2006 and December 2009.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: SETTING
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Ten neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) in New South Wales (NSW) and Australian Capital Territory (ACT), Australia.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: DESIGN
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data from the regional NICU database in NSW and ACT.

stage2_added_evidence.label: RESULTS
stage2_added_evidence.context: Of the 2170 infants who received surfactant, 1182 (54.5%) and 988 (45.5%) received early and late surfactant, respectively. The early surfactant group was less mature (27.1 ± 2.1 versus 29.4 ± 2.1 weeks) and had more CLD and mortality (40.2% versus 20.0%). The multivariable analysis showed early surfactant to be associated with less duration of ventilation, longer duration of CPAP and longer hospital stay but had little or no impact on CLD/mortality.
